Miami's bar scene is entering a new era of refinement. According to Eater Miami, the city's newest cocktail destinations are championing vermouth and sherry-based drinks alongside classic Spanish cocktails, marking a departure from Miami's historical emphasis on rum and agave spirits paired with citrus and exotic fruits.

This shift reflects Miami's geographic and cultural position as a gateway between the United States, the Caribbean, and Latin America. For decades, that role made the city a natural home for rum-forward drinks and agave-based cocktails that captured the flavors of the region. But as Miami's bar community matures, proprietors are exploring the deeper wells of European cocktail tradition, particularly the fortified wines and Spanish drinking culture that connect to the Caribbean's colonial history and ongoing cultural ties to Spain.

Vermouth, an aromatized fortified wine flavored with botanicals, has its roots in Turin, Italy, where modern versions were first produced in the mid- to late 18th century. Spanish sherry, produced in the Jerez region, represents another pillar of this new cocktail vocabulary. Both spirits share a complexity and subtlety that stands apart from the bolder, fruit-forward profiles that long dominated Miami drinking culture.

The timing of this evolution coincides with Miami's broader development as a major metropolitan center. The city proper is home to 442,241 residents according to the 2020 census, but the greater Miami metropolitan area encompasses an estimated 6.39 million people, making it the fifth-largest metropolitan area in the Southeast. With that growth has come a more diverse and sophisticated dining and drinking public, one increasingly interested in craft cocktails and traditional preparation methods.

The new bars emerging across Miami—details of which Eater Miami is documenting—suggest that the city's bartenders and owners are ready to build on the foundation of rum and agave tradition while incorporating European influences. This isn't a rejection of Miami's identity as a Caribbean and Latin American crossroads, but rather an expansion of it, inviting vermouth, sherry, and Spanish cocktail techniques into the conversation alongside the citrus and exotic fruits that have always defined the city's drink culture.

whatHappening: Four Seasons Miami has elevated its bar scene with Septimo & Nuna, two new upscale drinking destinations that blend sophisticated design with culinary excellence. These venues represent the luxury hotel chain's investment in creating high-end hospitality experiences that prioritize both ambiance and service.

articleBody:
Four Seasons Miami has introduced Septimo & Nuna, two distinctive bars designed to redefine upscale drinking in South Florida. The venues reflect a deliberate strategy by Four Seasons to create memorable hospitality experiences that extend beyond traditional hotel services, offering guests and locals alike access to curated spaces that combine design sophistication with culinary ambition.

According to Miami Curated, the best bars share common qualities: they are classically elegant, staffed with attentive service, and distinguished by special touches that elevate the ordinary drinking experience into something memorable. Septimo & Nuna appear to embody this philosophy, positioning themselves within the aesthetic and operational standards typically found in the world's finest landmark hotels.

Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts, headquartered in Toronto, has built its reputation on precisely this kind of curated excellence across its portfolio of more than 130 properties worldwide. The company's ownership structure—controlled since 2007 by Bill Gates through Cascade Investment and Saudi Prince Al-Waleed bin Talal through Kingdom Holding Company—reflects the deep resources and long-term vision required to maintain luxury standards globally. Miami represents a key market for this strategy, where affluent residents and international travelers expect world-class amenities.

The introduction of Septimo & Nuna at Four Seasons Miami demonstrates how luxury hospitality continues to compete not just on rooms and restaurants, but on creating Instagram-worthy, conversation-starting destinations within their properties. In an era where travelers seek authentic experiences and social currency, these bars serve as both functional venues and marketing assets that draw attention to the broader property.

For Miami's bar scene, the investment signals confidence in the city's continued appeal as a destination for high-end leisure. It also raises the competitive bar—literally—for other properties seeking to attract discerning guests who view drinking venues as essential components of their travel experience.

articleBody:

title: Miami Spice Back with New Reserve Tier and 300 Restaurants
summary: The 25th edition of Miami Spice Restaurant Months is back from August 1 through September 30, 2026. This year’s program from The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau (GMCVB) features three-course prix-fixe menus at a minimum of 30% savings at more than 300 participating…
whatHappening: Miami Spice Restaurant Month is returning for its 25th edition, running August 1 through September 30, 2026. The program now features a new reserve tier and expands to more than 300 participating restaurants offering three-course prix-fixe menus at minimum 30% savings.
whoInvolved: The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau (GMCVB) is organizing the program, a major promotional initiative designed to boost dining and tourism in the Miami area during the summer and early fall months.
whyMatters: The expansion to 300+ restaurants and introduction of a reserve tier signals growing restaurant participation and consumer interest in the program, making fine dining more accessible to locals and visitors during traditionally slower tourism seasons. The initiative drives economic activity across Miami's hospitality sector while establishing the region as a dining destination.
articleBody:
Miami's premier dining promotion is back for its silver anniversary. The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau is launching the 25th edition of Miami Spice Restaurant Month, running from August 1 through September 30, 2026. According to Miami Curated, the program features three-course prix-fixe menus at a minimum of 30% savings across more than 300 participating restaurants throughout the Miami area.

The 2026 edition marks a notable evolution for the program with the introduction of a new reserve tier, expanding options for diners seeking different price points and dining experiences. While specific details about the reserve tier's structure remain to be fully unveiled, the addition suggests the GMCVB is responding to demand from both high-end establishments and price-conscious diners looking to experience Miami's restaurant scene during the promotion.

Miami Spice has grown into one of the region's signature culinary events since its inception. The program strategically targets the slower summer and early fall months, a traditionally challenging period for the hospitality industry when tourists are less likely to visit South Florida due to heat and hurricane season. By offering substantial discounts on multi-course menus, the initiative drives foot traffic to restaurants that might otherwise see reduced business during this window.

The expansion to more than 300 restaurants represents significant participation from Miami's diverse dining community, ranging from casual eateries to fine dining establishments. This breadth allows both longtime residents and visitors to discover new culinary offerings while enjoying genuine savings on quality meals. The program has become instrumental in introducing diners to restaurants they might not otherwise try, often converting promotional visits into long-term patronage.

For Miami's tourism and hospitality sectors, Miami Spice serves dual purposes: it stimulates local dining activity during a slower season and reinforces the region's positioning as a world-class food destination. With a quarter-century of history and continued growth in participation, the program demonstrates sustained confidence from restaurateurs in its ability to drive meaningful business volume.

title: Where Elegance Lives: 5 Wonderful Miami Bars
summary: One of my go-to spots when I’m in New York City is the iconic King Cole Bar at the St. Regis. Stepping inside always feels like an immersion into a bygone era—a time when elegance was a deeply desired way of life. Even as modern fashion has shifted toward the casual, the bar…
whatHappening: Miami Curated has published a guide to five elegant bars in Miami, drawing inspiration from iconic cocktail establishments like the King Cole Bar at Manhattan's St. Regis Hotel. The piece celebrates venues that prioritize sophistication and timeless design in an era increasingly dominated by casual aesthetics.
whoInvolved: Miami Curated is a lifestyle publication focused on curated experiences in Miami. The article references the King Cole Bar at the St. Regis New York, a luxury hotel operated by Marriott International that has maintained five-star and five-diamond ratings since its 1904 completion.
whyMatters: The article highlights a niche but persistent market appetite for elegance and formal hospitality experiences, even as mainstream culture shifts toward casual dress and informality. This underscores the enduring appeal of upscale venues that offer an escape into refined atmospheres, particularly in a luxury tourism destination like Miami.
articleBody:
Miami's bar scene offers more than cocktails and conversation—it provides an entry point into a world where elegance remains not just alive but celebrated. According to Miami Curated, the city hosts several establishments that capture the timeless sophistication long associated with legendary cocktail bars in other major cities. One such inspiration comes from the King Cole Bar at the St. Regis in New York, where stepping through the doors transports visitors to a bygone era when formal dress and refined manners defined the hospitality experience.

The St. Regis New York itself represents the architectural and cultural pinnacle of luxury hotel design. Originally developed by John Jacob Astor IV and completed in 1904 under the designs of Trowbridge & Livingston, the hotel sits at a prestigious location at 2 East 55th Street at the corner of Fifth Avenue in Midtown Manhattan. Today, operated by Marriott International, it maintains Forbes five-star and AAA five-diamond ratings, making it a global standard for excellence in hospitality. The King Cole Bar within this landmark hotel exemplifies how a space can sustain an atmosphere of old-world glamour across generations.

Miami's curated bar selections aim to capture similar qualities—spaces where elegance is not merely tolerated but deeply desired and actively cultivated. These venues stand in contrast to the prevailing trend toward casual dining and drinking environments that have come to dominate urban hospitality. Yet their existence suggests that a dedicated clientele continues to seek out restaurants and bars where formality, craft, and attention to aesthetic detail remain paramount.

The rise of such establishments in Miami reflects the city's positioning as a destination for luxury experiences and high-end tourism. Miami's climate, cosmopolitan population, and real estate market have made it increasingly attractive to upscale hospitality brands and independent venues seeking to create sophisticated gathering spaces. Unlike casual bars designed around noise and volume, these establishments prioritize ambiance, service quality, and design heritage.

The enduring appeal of elegance-focused bars also speaks to a broader segment of travelers and residents who view hospitality not as mere transaction but as a form of cultural preservation. These spaces offer a counterpoint to the democratization of dining and drinking culture, maintaining standards and traditions that might otherwise be lost to market pressure for speed and affordability.

title: From Casual Lunch to Serious Dinner: Paperfish Sushi Brickell Stepped Up Its Game
summary: Paperfish Sushi Brickell has always been one of my “go to” places to have lunch or happy hour with a friend and they always like it. With all of the sushi restaurants in town you’d ask why Paperfish Sushi? The lovely décor that brightens up your day the moment you walk in,…
whatHappening: Paperfish Sushi Brickell, a long-standing casual lunch and happy hour destination in Miami, has elevated its offerings and atmosphere to compete in the city's competitive fine-dining sushi market. The restaurant is making a push toward more serious, upscale dining experiences while maintaining its original appeal.
whoInvolved: Paperfish Sushi Brickell is a sushi restaurant located in Miami's Brickell neighborhood, an area known for its concentration of restaurants and nightlife. The establishment has built a loyal customer base over time as a casual dining option.
whyMatters: The shift signals changing customer expectations in Miami's crowded sushi market, where restaurants must now offer both casual accessibility and elevated dining experiences to remain competitive. For a neighborhood establishment to successfully transition upward demonstrates growing demand for restaurants that can serve multiple occasions and clientele.
articleBody:
Paperfish Sushi Brickell has long occupied a comfortable niche in Miami's dining landscape as a reliable spot for casual lunches and after-work happy hours. The restaurant earned its reputation through consistent quality and an inviting atmosphere that made it an easy choice for colleagues meeting up or friends looking for an uncomplicated meal. But in a market saturated with sushi options, the restaurant recognized that survival—and growth—required evolution.

The restaurant's redesigned aesthetic is one of the first things customers notice. According to Miami Curated, the lovely décor that greets visitors as they walk through the door brightens up their day and sets a tone markedly more refined than the casual daytime experience. This attention to ambiance is crucial in a neighborhood like Brickell, where diners have seen increasing expectations for presentation and environment alongside quality food.

What distinguishes Paperfish's upgrade from simple redecorating is the underlying business logic. The sushi market in Miami is deeply competitive, with dozens of established restaurants vying for attention. Rather than abandon its core casual clientele, Paperfish positioned itself to capture occasions that demand more polish—date nights, client dinners, and special celebrations. By keeping the same location and much of its menu foundation, the restaurant preserved the loyalty of regular lunch-goers while signaling to the broader market that it belonged in serious dining conversations too.

The restaurant's ability to shift its positioning without losing its original identity suggests a successful understanding of its market. Loyal customers who enjoyed casual lunches continue to have that option, while the elevated evening experience opens doors to customers who might never have considered Paperfish for anything beyond a quick workday meal. This flexibility is increasingly valuable in neighborhood restaurants, where demographic changes and shifting work patterns demand adaptability.

For Miami's Brickell area specifically, Paperfish's transformation reflects broader evolution in the neighborhood's dining culture. As the area continues to attract both corporate workers and residential growth, restaurants must serve both the weekday lunch crowd and weekend diners seeking memorable experiences. Paperfish's move from casual-only to casual-and-upscale places it squarely in that middle ground—accessible enough for regulars, polished enough for occasions.
